title: Redis Caching Patterns: Scaling Backend Architecture ⚡
ig_caption:
Redis Caching Patterns: Scaling Backend Architecture ⚡ — how cache-aside handles DB latency
and stops overload when traffic spikes.

• Same 14 users + same database
• USERS: 14 requests
• No cache: every request hits the DB → DB overload ✗
• Redis cache: most reads served from memory → DB barely touched ✓

Under the hood (cache-aside):
1) Read key from Redis
2) If missing, fetch from DB
3) Write result back to Redis with TTL
4) Future requests avoid the DB

Practical takeaway: In interviews, call out TTL + cache invalidation strategy (and what happens on misses).

Would you rather optimize for consistency or latency first: strict reads or eventual freshness?

fb_caption:
Redis Cache vs No Cache—same workload, different outcomes.

In this VIZ: 14 users send 14 requests to the same database.
- No cache: every request hits the DB → DB overload and latency spikes (✗)
- With Redis cache: reads are served from in-memory entries → DB is barely touched (✓)

Architecture trade-offs (production reality):
1) Latency: Redis reduces database round-trips, especially for hot keys.
2) Load shedding: caching smooths bursts; your DB doesn’t get “thundering herd” traffic.
3) Consistency: stale data risk depends on TTL and invalidation approach.
4) Failure modes: define behavior on cache misses, cache failures, and Redis outages.

Common patterns to mention in system design interview answers:
- Cache-aside (lazy): read-through Redis; on miss, load from DB and populate Redis.
- Write-through: write to cache and DB simultaneously (more write cost).
- Write-back: update cache first, persist asynchronously (more complex + risk).

Rule of thumb: pair caching with clear TTL, invalidation rules, and a “graceful degrade” path (e.g., serve from DB if Redis is down).
